claim: In all three environments, previous category-dependent psychometric functions were shifted horizontally, indicative of a history bias.
source: In all three environments, previous category-dependent psychometric functions were shifted horizontally, indicative of a history bias (repetitive: t=8.133, p<10–4, neutral: t=4.218, p=0.0002, alternating: t=–2.276, p=0.0287; two-tailed t tests).
evidence: Statistical test results and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The psychometric function shifts pointed in opposite directions for the two structured environments, with a strong tendency to repeat the previous category in repetitive and a tendency to alternate the previous category in alternating.
source: Critically, these shifts pointed in opposite directions for the two structured environments, with a strong tendency to repeat the previous category in repetitive and a tendency to alternate the previous category in alternating
evidence: Direct statement about observed pattern in data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The previous stimulus category had no effect on perceptual sensitivity.
source: The previous stimulus category had no effect on perceptual sensitivity (history-dependent psychometric slopes: repetitive: t=–0.0397, p=0.969, Bf10=0.175, neutral: t=–0.623, p=0.537, Bf10=0.209, alternating: t=0.094, p=0.926, Bf10=0.175; two-tailed t tests and Bayes factors).
evidence: Statistical test results including Bayes factors supporting null hypothesis.

claim: The impact of the previous trial stimulus category on current choice was different from zero in all three environments, including neutral.
source: The impact of the previous trial stimulus category on current choice was different from zero in all three environments, including neutral (Figure 1D; repetitive: p<10–5; alternating: p=0.0003; neutral: p=0.0002; two-tailed permutation tests).
evidence: Statistical test results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In both biased environments, the impact of previous stimulus category was different from neutral and shifted in opposite directions.
source: But critically, in both biased environments, this impact was different from neutral and shifted in opposite directions, indicating a tendency to repeat the previous stimulus category in repetitive and vice versa in alternating (Figure 1D; repetitive vs. neutral: p<10–5; alternating vs. neutral: p<10–5; two-tailed permutation tests).
evidence: Statistical test results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The impact of the previous choice on the current choice tended to be overall weaker, more idiosyncratic, and less systematically related to the sensory environment than the impact of the previous stimulus.
source: The impact of the previous choice on the current choice tended to be overall weaker, more idiosyncratic, and less systematically related to the sensory environment than the impact of the previous stimulus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Direct statement about observed pattern in data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The shift in stimulus weights between each biased condition and neutral was significantly larger than the corresponding shift in choice weights.
source: Indeed, the shift in stimulus weights between each biased condition and neutral was significantly larger than the corresponding shift in choice weights (repetitive p=0.0002, alternating: p=0.0026; two-tailed permutation test).
evidence: Statistical test results comparing different weight shifts.

claim: There was little contribution of the stimulus categories from trials further back in time.
source: There was little contribution of the stimulus categories from trials further back in time (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Direct statement about observed pattern in data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

source: Both factors uniquely predicted performance (sensitivity: r=0.798, p<0.0001; bias adjustment: r=0.493, p=0.0026; Pearson correlation)

evidence: Direct statement about analysis results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.
